questions.enonce_markdown: a) Differentiate between a prophet (Al-nabi) and a Rasul (Messenger) in Islam. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: A **prophet (nabi)** is a man chosen by God who receives revelation to guide people to worship God and to follow the earlier teaching. He often renews the message of an earlier messenger, and need not bring a new book or a new law. A **Rasul (messenger)** is a prophet who is sent with a specific mission to a people, usually with a new scripture or a new law, and who calls them to believe, so he also meets rejection from his people. Muslim scholars generally say that every Rasul is a nabi but not every nabi is a Rasul. Examples of messengers who brought a scripture are Musa (the Tawrat), Dawud (the Zabur), Isa (the Injil) and Muhammad (the Qur'an). Scholars differ somewhat on the exact criteria, and Muslims believe in all prophets and messengers without distinction.

questions.enonce_markdown: b) How great is prophet Muhammad (S.A.S) among the prophets of Allah? (20 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Muslims believe that Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the last prophet and messenger of God. The Qur'an and the tradition describe his greatness in several ways, though Muslims also hold that all prophets deserve respect and make no distinction between them.

**1. The seal of the prophets.** The Qur'an calls him the "Seal of the Prophets": Muslims believe that prophecy was completed with him and that no prophet will come after him. His message therefore confirms and completes the earlier ones.

**2. A universal message.** Earlier prophets are believed to have been sent to their own peoples, whereas Muhammad was sent to all humankind. The Qur'an calls him "a mercy to all the worlds".

**3. The Qur'an as a lasting miracle.** The revelation given to him is the Qur'an, whose language and message Muslims regard as inimitable, and which they believe is preserved in its original form. Miracles of earlier prophets were tied to their time; his main miracle remains.

**4. Moral character and example.** Before his call he was known as "al-Amin" (the trustworthy). The Qur'an describes him as being of "a great moral character" and as an excellent example. His life in Makkah and Madinah, as husband, father, leader, judge and neighbour, is the model for Muslims.

**5. Spiritual honour.** According to Islamic tradition, he made the night journey (Isra) from Makkah to Jerusalem and ascended through the heavens (Mi'raj), where the five daily prayers were prescribed. Muslims also believe that he will have a special role of intercession on the Last Day.

**6. Achievements as leader.** He guided the community from persecution in Makkah to a state in Madinah, where he issued the covenant between the Muslims and other groups, established justice and consultation, and returned to Makkah peacefully. In about twenty-three years he transformed Arabia, and Islam spread widely after him.

**7. The Final Sermon and complete religion.** In his farewell sermon he stressed the equality of people, the rights of women, the sanctity of life and property, and the prohibition of usury. The Qur'an says that the religion was completed for the Muslims.

**8. Limits of the claim.** Muslims do not regard Muhammad as divine, nor as above God's other prophets in worship. They believe in Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and others and honour them. His greatness is in his role, his message and his example.

**Conclusion.** For Muslims Muhammad is the greatest of the prophets in the sense that he is the last, the universal messenger, the bearer of the Qur'an, and the supreme example, while he remains a human servant and messenger of God.
